{{short description|Higher probability of publishing results showing a significant finding}}
{{distinguish|Reporting bias|Media bias}}

In published academic [[research]], '''publication bias''' occurs when the outcome of an experiment or research study [[bias]]es the decision to publish or otherwise distribute it. Publishing only results that show a [[Statistical significance|significant]] finding disturbs the balance of findings in favor of positive results.<ref name="Song2010">{{Cite journal | last1 = Song | first1 = F. | last2 = Parekh | first2 = S. | last3 = Hooper | first3 = L. | last4 = Loke | first4 = Y. K. | last5 = Ryder | first5 = J. | last6 = Sutton | first6 = A. J. | last7 = Hing | first7 = C. | last8 = Kwok | first8 = C. S. | last9 = Pang | first9 = C. | last10 = Harvey | first10 = I. | title = Dissemination and publication of research findings: An updated review of related biases | journal = Health Technology Assessment | volume = 14 | issue = 8 | pages = iii, iix–xi, iix–193 | year = 2010 | doi = 10.3310/hta14080 | pmid = 20181324 | doi-access = free | hdl = 2381/16613 | hdl-access = free }}</ref> The study of publication bias is an important topic in [[metascience]].

Despite similar quality of execution and [[Design of experiments|design]],<ref name=Easterbrook>{{cite journal |last1=Easterbrook |first1=P. J. |last2=Berlin |first2=J. A. |last3=Gopalan |first3=R. |last4=Matthews |first4=D. R. |s2cid=36570135 |title=Publication bias in clinical research |journal=[[Lancet (journal)|Lancet]] |year=1991 |volume=337 |issue=8746 |pages=867–872 |doi=10.1016/0140-6736(91)90201-Y |pmid=1672966|doi-access=free }}</ref> papers with statistically significant results are three times more likely to be published than those with [[null result]]s.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Dickersin |first1=K. |author-link=Kay Dickersin|last2=Chan |first2=S. |last3=Chalmers |first3=T. C. |title=Publication bias and clinical trials |journal=[[Controlled Clinical Trials]] |year=1987 |volume=8 |issue=4 |pages=343–353 |doi=10.1016/0197-2456(87)90155-3 |display-authors=etal |pmid=3442991}}</ref> This unduly motivates researchers to manipulate their practices to ensure statistically significant results, such as by [[data dredging]].<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Pearce|first1=J|last2=Derrick|first2=B|title= Preliminary testing: The devil of statistics?|journal= Reinvention: An International Journal of Undergraduate Research |date=2019|volume=12|issue=2|doi=10.31273/reinvention.v12i2.339|doi-access=free}}</ref>

Many factors contribute to publication bias.<ref name="Rothstein2005" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Chopra |first1=Felix |last2=Haaland |first2=Ingar |last3=Roth |first3=Christopher |last4=Stegmann |first4=Andreas |date=2023 |title=The Null Result Penalty |journal=The Economic Journal |volume=134 |issue=657 |pages=193–219 |doi=10.1093/ej/uead060 |issn=0013-0133}}</ref> For instance, once a scientific finding is well established, it may become newsworthy to publish reliable papers that fail to reject the [[null hypothesis]].<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Luijendijk|first1=HJ|last2=Koolman|first2=X|title=The incentive to publish negative studies: how beta-blockers and depression got stuck in the publication cycle.|journal=J Clin Epidemiol|date=May 2012|volume=65|issue=5|pages=488–92|doi=10.1016/j.jclinepi.2011.06.022|pmid=22342262}}</ref> Most commonly, investigators simply decline to submit results, leading to [[non-response bias]]. Investigators may also assume they made a mistake, find that the null result fails to support a known finding, lose interest in the topic, or anticipate that others will be uninterested in the null results.<ref name="Easterbrook" />

Attempts to find unpublished studies often prove difficult or are unsatisfactory.<ref name="Rothstein2005">H. Rothstein, A. J. Sutton and M. Borenstein. (2005). ''Publication bias in meta-analysis: prevention, assessment and adjustments''. Wiley. Chichester, England; Hoboken, NJ.</ref> In an effort to combat this problem, some journals require that authors [[Preregistration (science)|preregister]] their methods and analyses, ''prior'' to collecting data, with organizations like the [[Center for Open Science]].

Other proposed strategies to detect and control for publication bias<ref name="Rothstein2005" /> include [[p-curve]] analysis<ref>{{Cite journal|title =  P-curve: A key to the file-drawer.|journal =   Journal of Experimental Psychology: General| doi=10.1037/a0033242|pmid =   23855496|volume=143|issue =   2|pages=534–547|year =  2014|last1 =  Simonsohn|first1 =  Uri|last2 =   Nelson|first2 =   Leif D.|last3 =   Simmons|first3 =   Joseph P.|s2cid = 8505270}}</ref> and disfavoring small and non-randomized studies due to high susceptibility to error and bias.<ref name="Easterbrook" />

==Definition==
Publication bias occurs when the publication of research results depends not just on the quality of the research but also on the hypothesis tested, and the significance and direction of effects detected.<ref>{{Cite journal |author=K. Dickersin |title=The existence of publication bias and risk factors for its occurrence |journal=[[JAMA (journal)|JAMA]] |date=March 1990 |volume=263 |issue=10 |pages=1385–9|pmid=2406472 |doi=10.1001/jama.263.10.1385}}</ref> The subject was first discussed in 1959 by statistician Theodore Sterling to refer to fields in which "successful" research is more likely to be published. As a result, "the literature of such a field consists in substantial part of false conclusions resulting from errors of the first kind in statistical tests of significance".<ref>{{cite journal |last=Sterling |first=Theodore D. |title=Publication decisions and their possible effects on inferences drawn from tests of significance—or vice versa |journal=Journal of the American Statistical Association |date=March 1959 |volume=54 |pages=30–34 |doi=10.2307/2282137 |issue=285|jstor=2282137 }}</ref> In the worst case, false conclusions could canonize as being true if the publication rate of negative results is too low.<ref>{{cite journal |last1 = Nissen |first1 = Silas Boye |last2 = Magidson| first2 = Tali| last3 = Gross| first3 = Kevin | last4 = Bergstrom| first4 = Carl |title=Research: Publication bias and the canonization of false facts |journal=eLife |date=December 20, 2016 |volume=5 |article-number=e21451 |doi=10.7554/eLife.21451 |pmid = 27995896 |pmc = 5173326 |arxiv= 1609.00494 |doi-access = free }}</ref>

One effect of publication bias is sometimes called the '''file-drawer effect''', or '''file-drawer problem'''. This term suggests that negative results, those that do not support the initial hypotheses of researchers are often "filed away" and go no further than the researchers' file drawers, leading to a bias in published research.<ref>{{Cite journal |author=Jeffrey D. Scargle |title=Publication bias: the "file-drawer problem" in scientific inference |url= https://www.scientificexploration.org/docs/14/jse_14_1_scargle.pdf |journal=[[Journal of Scientific Exploration]] |volume=14 |issue=1 |pages=91–106 |year=2000|bibcode=1999physics...9033S |arxiv=physics/9909033 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Moniz |first1=Philip |last2=Druckman |first2=James N. |last3=Freese |first3=Jeremy |date=2025 |title=The file drawer problem in social science survey experiments |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=122 |issue=12 |article-number=e2426937122 |doi=10.1073/pnas.2426937122|pmid=40106354 |pmc=11962440 |bibcode=2025PNAS..12226937M }}</ref> The term "file drawer problem" was coined by psychologist [[Robert Rosenthal (psychologist)|Robert Rosenthal]] in 1979.<ref>{{cite journal | author = Rosenthal R | year = 1979 | title = File drawer problem and tolerance for null results | journal = Psychol Bull | volume = 86 | issue = 3| pages = 638–41 | doi=10.1037/0033-2909.86.3.638| s2cid = 36070395 }}</ref>

Positive-results bias, a type of publication bias, occurs when authors are more likely to submit, or editors are more likely to accept, positive results than negative or inconclusive results.<ref>{{Cite journal |author=D.L. Sackett |title=Bias in analytic research |journal=[[Journal of Chronic Diseases|J Chronic Dis]] |year=1979 |volume=32 |issue=1–2 |pmid=447779 |pages=51–63 |doi=10.1016/0021-9681(79)90012-2}}</ref> Outcome reporting bias occurs when multiple outcomes are measured and analyzed, but the reporting of these outcomes is dependent on the strength and direction of its results. A generic term coined to describe these post-hoc choices is [[HARKing]] ("Hypothesizing After the Results are Known").<ref>{{Cite journal |author=N.L. Kerr |title=HARKing: Hypothesizing After the Results are Known |journal=[[Personality and Social Psychology Review]] |year=1998 |volume=2 |issue=3 |pages=196–217 |url=https://www2.psych.ubc.ca/~schaller/528Readings/Kerr1998.pdf |doi=10.1207/s15327957pspr0203_4 |pmid=15647155|doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Evidence==
[[File:FloreAndWicherts2015 meta analysis sex stereotype threat.png|thumb|Funnel plot of a meta-analysis of [[stereotype threat]] on girls' math scores showing asymmetry typical of publication bias. From Flore, P. C., & Wicherts, J. M. (2015)<ref name="Flore2015">{{cite journal |author1=Flore P. C. |author2=Wicherts J. M. | year = 2015 | title = Does stereotype threat influence performance of girls in stereotyped domains? A meta-analysis | doi = 10.1016/j.jsp.2014.10.002 | journal = J Sch Psychol | volume = 53 | issue = 1| pages = 25–44 | pmid=25636259}}</ref>]]

In the biomedical field, there is extensive [[meta-research]] on publication bias. Investigators who followed clinical trials from the submission of their protocols to ethics committees (or regulatory authorities) until the publication of their results observed that those with positive results are more likely to be published. This has been noted across multiple studies.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Dickersin| first1 = K.| last2 = Min | first2 = Y.I. | title = NIH clinical trials and publication bias| journal = Online J Curr Clin Trials| volume = Doc No 50| pages = [4967 words; 53 paragraphs]| date = 1993| pmid = 8306005|issn=1059-2725|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/14893304}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Decullier E, Lheritier V, Chapuis F | year = 2005 | title = Fate of biomedical research protocols and publication bias in France: retrospective cohort study | journal = BMJ | volume = 331 | issue = 7507| pages = 19–22 | doi=10.1136/bmj.38488.385995.8f| pmid = 15967761 | pmc = 558532 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Song F, Parekh-Bhurke S, Hooper L, Loke Y, Ryder J, Sutton A | year = 2009 | title = Extent of publication bias in different categories of research cohorts: a meta-analysis of empirical studies | journal = BMC Med Res Methodol | volume = 9 | article-number = 79 | doi=10.1186/1471-2288-9-79| pmid = 19941636 | pmc = 2789098 |display-authors=etal | doi-access = free }}</ref>

Additionally, when comparing study protocols with published articles, research has demonstrated that studies often fail to report negative results when published.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Chan AW, Altman DG | year = 2005 | title = Identifying outcome reporting bias in randomised trials on PubMed: review of publications and survey of authors | journal = BMJ | volume = 330 | issue = 7494| page = 753 | doi=10.1136/bmj.38356.424606.8f | pmid=15681569 | pmc=555875}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Riveros C, Dechartres A, Perrodeau E, Haneef R, Boutron I, Ravaud P | year = 2013 | title = Timing and completeness of trial results posted at ClinicalTrials.gov and published in journals | journal = PLOS Med | volume = 10 | issue = 12| article-number = e1001566 | doi=10.1371/journal.pmed.1001566| pmid = 24311990 | pmc = 3849189 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

The presence of publication bias has also been investigated in [[meta-analyses]]. The largest such analysis examined systematic reviews of medical treatments from the [[Cochrane Library]].<ref name="kicinski2015">{{Cite journal | pmid = 25988604| year = 2015| last1 = Kicinski| first1 = M| title = Publication bias in meta-analyses from the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews| journal = Statistics in Medicine| pages = 2781–93| last2 = Springate| first2 = D. A.| last3 = Kontopantelis| first3 = E| doi = 10.1002/sim.6525| volume=34| issue = 20| s2cid = 25560005}}</ref> The study showed that statistically positive significant findings are 27% more likely to be included in meta-analyses of efficacy than other findings. Furthermore, results showing no evidence of adverse effects have a 78% greater probability of inclusion in safety studies than statistically significant results showing adverse effects. Evidence of publication bias was found in meta-analyses published in prominent medical journals.<ref>{{cite journal | author = Kicinski M | year = 2013 | title = Publication bias in recent meta-analyses | journal = PLOS ONE | volume = 8 | issue = 11| article-number = e81823 | doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0081823| pmid = 24363797 | pmc = 3868709 | bibcode = 2013PLoSO...881823K | doi-access = free }}</ref>

Meta-analyses have also been performed in the field of ecology and environmental biology. In a study of 100 meta-analyses in ecology, only 49% tested for publication bias.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Nakagawa |first1=Shinichi |last2=Santos |first2=Eduardo S. A. |date=2012-09-01 |title=Methodological issues and advances in biological meta-analysis |journal=Evolutionary Ecology |language=en |volume=26 |issue=5 |pages=1253–1274 |doi=10.1007/s10682-012-9555-5 |bibcode=2012EvEco..26.1253N |s2cid=254466150 |issn=1573-8477}}</ref> While multiple tests have been developed to detect publication bias, most perform poorly in the field of ecology because of high levels of heterogeneity in the data and that often observations are not fully independent.<ref name=":03">{{Cite journal |last1=Nakagawa |first1=Shinichi |last2=Lagisz |first2=Malgorzata |last3=Jennions |first3=Michael D. |last4=Koricheva |first4=Julia |last5=Noble |first5=Daniel W. A. |last6=Parker |first6=Timothy H. |last7=Sánchez-Tójar |first7=Alfredo |last8=Yang |first8=Yefeng |last9=O'Dea |first9=Rose E. |date=January 2022 |title=Methods for testing publication bias in ecological and evolutionary meta-analyses |url=https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/2041-210X.13724 |journal=Methods in Ecology and Evolution |language=en |volume=13 |issue=1 |pages=4–21 |doi=10.1111/2041-210X.13724 |bibcode=2022MEcEv..13....4N |hdl=1885/294436 |s2cid=241159497 |issn=2041-210X|hdl-access=free }}</ref>

A review of published outcomes studying acupuncture treatment found that as of 1998, "No trial published in China or Russia/USSR found a test treatment to be ineffective."<ref name="Vickers Goyal Harland Rees 1998 pp. 159–166">{{cite journal | last1=Vickers | first1=Andrew | last2=Goyal | first2=Niraj | last3=Harland | first3=Robert | last4=Rees | first4=Rebecca | title=Do Certain Countries Produce Only Positive Results? A Systematic Review of Controlled Trials | journal=Controlled Clinical Trials | volume=19 | issue=2 | date=1998 | doi=10.1016/S0197-2456(97)00150-5 | pages=159–166| pmid=9551280 }}</ref>

==Impact on meta-analysis==
Where publication bias is present, published studies are no longer a representative sample of the available evidence. This bias distorts the results of meta-analyses and [[systematic review]]s. For example, [[evidence-based medicine]] is increasingly reliant on meta-analysis to assess evidence.

[[File:Fig forestplot v1.3.jpg|thumb|upright=1.8|Conceptual illustration of how publication bias affects effect estimates in a meta-analysis. When negative effects are not published, the overall effect estimate tends to be inflated. From Nilsonne (2023).<ref name="Nilsonne2023">{{cite journal |author1 = Nilsonne G. | year = 2023 | title = Figure: Publication bias | doi = 10.53962/w0d6-9kwa | journal = ResearchEquals| doi-access = free }}</ref>]]

Meta-analyses and systematic reviews can account for publication bias by including evidence from unpublished studies and the grey literature. The presence of publication bias can also be explored by constructing a [[funnel plot]] in which the estimate of the reported effect size is plotted against a measure of precision or sample size. The premise is that the scatter of points should reflect a funnel shape, indicating that the reporting of effect sizes is not related to their statistical significance.<ref name=":0" /> However, when small studies are predominately in one direction (usually the direction of larger effect sizes), asymmetry will ensue and this may be indicative of publication bias.<ref>{{Cite book<!-- no bot --> |url=https://archive.org/details/summingupscience00ligh|date=1984 |isbn=978-0-674-85430-7 |oclc=1036880624|url-access=registration|publisher=Harvard University Press|location=Cambridge, Mass.|doi=10.2307/j.ctvk12px9|title=Summing Up: The Science of Reviewing Research |last1=Light |first1=Richard J. |last2=Pillemer |first2=David B.|pp=[https://books.google.com/books?id=bIf8kktfgCYC&pg=PA65 65ff] }}</ref>

Because an inevitable degree of subjectivity exists in the interpretation of funnel plots, several tests have been proposed for detecting funnel plot asymmetry.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last1=Debray|first1=Thomas P.A.|last2=Moons|first2=Karel G.M.|last3=Riley|first3=Richard D.|title=Detecting small-study effects and funnel plot asymmetry in meta-analysis of survival data: a comparison of new and existing tests|journal=Research Synthesis Methods|volume=9|issue=1|language=en|pages=41–50|doi=10.1002/jrsm.1266|pmid=28975717|pmc=5873397|issn=1759-2887|year=2018}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Jin|first1=Zhi-Chao|last2=Zhou|first2=Xiao-Hua|last3=He|first3=Jia|date=2015-01-30|title=Statistical methods for dealing with publication bias in meta-analysis|journal=Statistics in Medicine|language=en|volume=34|issue=2|pages=343–360|doi=10.1002/sim.6342|pmid=25363575|s2cid=12341436 |issn=1097-0258}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Rücker|first1=Gerta|last2=Carpenter|first2=James R.|last3=Schwarzer|first3=Guido|date=2011-03-01|title=Detecting and adjusting for small-study effects in meta-analysis|journal=Biometrical Journal|language=en|volume=53|issue=2|pages=351–368|doi=10.1002/bimj.201000151|pmid=21374698|s2cid=24560718 |issn=1521-4036}}</ref> These are often based on linear regression including the popular [[Matthias Egger|Eggers]] regression test,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Egger |first1=M. |last2=Smith |first2=G. D. |last3=Schneider |first3=M. |last4=Minder |first4=C. |date=1997-09-13 |title=Bias in meta-analysis detected by a simple, graphical test |journal=BMJ |language=en |volume=315 |issue=7109 |pages=629–634 |doi=10.1136/bmj.315.7109.629 |issn=0959-8138 |pmc=2127453 |pmid=9310563}}</ref> and may adopt a multiplicative or additive dispersion parameter to adjust for the presence of between-study heterogeneity. Some approaches may even attempt to compensate for the (potential) presence of publication bias,<ref name="kicinski2015" /><ref>{{cite journal|author=Silliman N|year=1997|title=Hierarchical selection models with applications in meta-analysis|journal=Journal of the American Statistical Association|volume=92|issue=439|pages=926–936|doi=10.1080/01621459.1997.10474047}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|year=1996|title=Estimating effect size under publication bias: small sample properties and robustness of a random effects selection model|journal=Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics|volume=21|issue=4|pages=299–332|doi=10.3102/10769986021004299|vauthors=Hedges L, Vevea J|s2cid=123680599}}</ref> which is particularly useful to explore the potential impact on meta-analysis results.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=McShane|first1=Blakeley B.|last2=Böckenholt|first2=Ulf|last3=Hansen|first3=Karsten T.|date=2016-09-29|title=Adjusting for Publication Bias in Meta-Analysis|journal=Perspectives on Psychological Science|language=en|volume=11|issue=5|pages=730–749|doi=10.1177/1745691616662243|pmid=27694467|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|year=2000|title=Modelling publication bias in meta-analysis: a review|journal=Stat Methods Med Res|volume=9|issue=5|pages=421–445|doi=10.1191/096228000701555244|vauthors=Sutton AJ, Song F, Gilbody SM, Abrams KR|doi-broken-date=10 July 2025 |hdl=2381/22970|hdl-access=free}}</ref><ref name="kicinski2014">{{Cite journal|last1=Kicinski|first1=M|year=2014|title=How does under-reporting of negative and inconclusive results affect the false-positive rate in meta-analysis? A simulation study|journal=BMJ Open|volume=4|issue=8|article-number=e004831|doi=10.1136/bmjopen-2014-004831|doi-access=free|pmc=4156818|pmid=25168036}}</ref>

In ecology and environmental biology, a study found that publication bias impacted the effect size, statistical power, and magnitude. The prevalence of publication bias distorted confidence in meta-analytic results, with 66% of initially statistically significant meta-analytic means becoming non-significant after correcting for publication bias.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Yang |first1=Yefeng |last2=Sánchez-Tójar |first2=Alfredo |last3=O'Dea |first3=Rose E. |last4=Noble |first4=Daniel W. A. |last5=Koricheva |first5=Julia |last6=Jennions |first6=Michael D. |last7=Parker |first7=Timothy H. |last8=Lagisz |first8=Malgorzata |last9=Nakagawa |first9=Shinichi |date=2023-04-03 |title=Publication bias impacts on effect size, statistical power, and magnitude (Type M) and sign (Type S) errors in ecology and evolutionary biology |journal=BMC Biology |volume=21 |issue=1 |page=71 |doi=10.1186/s12915-022-01485-y |issn=1741-7007 |pmc=10071700 |pmid=37013585 |doi-access=free }}</ref> Ecological and evolutionary studies consistently had low statistical power (15%) with a 4-fold exaggeration of effects on average (Type M error rates = 4.4).

The presence of publication bias can be detected by Time-lag bias tests, where time-lag bias occurs when larger or statistically significant effects are published more quickly than smaller or non-statistically significant effects. It can manifest as a decline in the magnitude of the overall effect over time. The key feature of time-lag bias tests is that, as more studies accumulate, the mean effect size is expected to converge on its true value.<ref name=":03"/>

==Compensation examples==
Two meta-analyses of the efficacy of [[reboxetine]] as an [[antidepressant]] demonstrated attempts to detect publication bias in clinical trials. Based on positive trial data, reboxetine was originally passed as a treatment for depression in many countries in Europe and the UK in 2001 (though in practice it is rarely used for this indication). A 2010 meta-analysis concluded that reboxetine was ineffective and that the preponderance of positive-outcome trials reflected publication bias, mostly due to trials published by the drug manufacturer [[Pfizer]]. A subsequent meta-analysis published in 2011, based on the original data, found flaws in the 2010 analyses and suggested that the data indicated reboxetine was effective in severe depression (see [[Reboxetine#Efficacy|Reboxetine § Efficacy]]). Examples of publication bias are given by [[Ben Goldacre]]<ref>{{Cite speech |url=https://www.ted.com/talks/ben_goldacre_what_doctors_don_t_know_about_the_drugs_they_prescribe |title=What doctors don't know about the drugs they prescribe |last=Goldacre |first=Ben |language=en |access-date=2020-02-03|date=June 2012|event=[[TEDMED]] 2012 }}</ref> and [[Peter Wilmshurst]].<ref>{{Cite journal <!-- no bot -->|doi = 10.1258/rsmmlj.75.1.3|pmid = 17506338|title = Dishonesty in Medical Research|journal = Medico-Legal Journal|volume = 75|issue = 1|pages = 3–12|year = 2007|last1 = Wilmshurst|first1 = Peter|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20130521050439/http://www.medico-legalsociety.org.uk/articles/dishonesty_in_medical_research.pdf|archive-date = 2013-05-21|url = https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/f8a05504a870d927eebcfaae5b1fa6e663a092df|s2cid = 26915448}}</ref>

In the social sciences, a study of published papers exploring the relationship between corporate social and financial performance found that "in economics, finance, and accounting journals, the average correlations were only about half the magnitude of the findings published in Social Issues Management, Business Ethics, or Business and Society journals".<ref>{{Cite journal | doi=10.5840/beq201121325| title=Institutional Logics in the Study of Organizations: The Social Construction of the Relationship between Corporate Social and Financial Performance| journal=Business Ethics Quarterly| volume=21| issue=3| pages=409–444| year=2011| last1=Orlitzky| first1=Marc| s2cid=147466849|url= http://marcorlitzky.webs.com/Papers/Orlitzky2011beq_preprint.pdf| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180125074628/http://marcorlitzky.webs.com/Papers/Orlitzky2011beq_preprint.pdf| archive-date=2018-01-25}}</ref>

One example cited as an instance of publication bias is the refusal to publish attempted replications of Bem's work that claimed evidence for precognition by ''[[Journal of Personality and Social Psychology|The Journal of Personality and Social Psychology]]'' (the original publisher of Bem's article).<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2011/apr/23/ben-goldacre-bad-science |title=Backwards step on looking into the future |first=Ben |last=Goldacre |work=The Guardian |date=23 April 2011 |access-date=11 April 2017}}</ref>

An analysis<ref>{{cite journal | first1= Zhenglun |last1=Pan |first2=Thomas A. |last2=Trikalinos |first3=Fotini K. |last3=Kavvoura |first4=Joseph |last4=Lau |first5=John P.A. |last5=Ioannidis |author-link5=John P.A. Ioannidis | year = 2005 | title = Local literature bias in genetic epidemiology: An empirical evaluation of the Chinese literature | doi = 10.1371/journal.pmed.0020334 | pmid = 16285839 | pmc = 1285066 | journal = [[PLOS Medicine]] | volume = 2 | issue = 12| article-number = e334 | doi-access = free }}</ref> comparing studies of gene-disease associations originating in China to those originating outside China found that those conducted within the country reported a stronger association and a more statistically significant result.<ref>{{cite journal | author = Ling Tang Jin | year = 2005 | title = Selection Bias in Meta-Analyses of Gene-Disease Associations | doi = 10.1371/journal.pmed.0020409 | pmid = 16363911 | pmc = 1285067 | journal = [[PLOS Medicine]] | volume = 2 | issue = 12| article-number = e409 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

==Risks==
[[John Ioannidis]] argues that "claimed research findings may often be simply accurate measures of the prevailing bias."<ref name="pmid16060722">{{cite journal |author = Ioannidis J|author-link = John P. A. Ioannidis|title = Why most published research findings are false|journal = PLOS Med|volume = 2|issue = 8|article-number = e124|year = 2005|pmid = 16060722|doi = 10.1371/journal.pmed.0020124|pmc = 1182327 | doi-access=free }}</ref> He lists the following factors as those that make a paper with a positive result more likely to enter the literature and suppress negative-result papers:
* The studies conducted in a field have small sample sizes.
* [[effect size|The effect size]]s in a field tend to be smaller.
* There is both a greater number and lesser preselection of tested relationships.
* There is greater flexibility in designs, definitions, outcomes, and analytical modes.
* There are prejudices (financial interest, political, or otherwise).
* The scientific field is hot and there are more scientific teams pursuing publication.

Other factors include [[Experimenter's bias|experimenter bias]] and [[white hat bias]].

==Remedies==
Publication bias can be contained through better-powered studies, enhanced research standards, and careful consideration of true and non-true relationships.<ref name="pmid16060722" /> Better-powered studies refer to large studies that deliver definitive results or test major concepts and lead to low-bias meta-analysis. Enhanced research standards such as the pre-registration of protocols, the registration of data collections, and adherence to established protocols are other techniques. To avoid false-positive results, the experimenter must consider the chances that they are testing a true or non-true relationship. This can be undertaken by properly assessing the false positive report probability based on the statistical power of the test<ref name="FalsePositiveProbability">{{cite journal|last2=Chanock|first2=S|last3=Garcia-Closas|first3=M|last4=El Ghormli|first4=L|last5=Rothman|first5=N|date=March 2004|title=Assessing the Probability That a Positive Report is False: An Approach for Molecular Epidemiology Studies|journal=[[JNCI]]|volume=96|issue=6|pages=434–42|doi=10.1093/jnci/djh075|pmid=15026468|author=Wacholder, S.|pmc=7713993|doi-access=free}}</ref> and reconfirming (whenever ethically acceptable) established findings of prior studies known to have minimal bias.

Statistical corrections for publication bias include funnel-plot meta-regressions and selection models.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Stanley |first1=T. D. |last2=Doucouliagos |first2=Hristos |year=2014 |title=Meta-regression approximations to reduce publication selection bias |journal=Research Synthesis Methods |volume=5 |issue=1 |pages=60–78 |doi=10.1002/jrsm.1095}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Andrews |first1=Isaiah |last2=Kasy |first2=Maximilian |year=2019 |title=Identification of and Correction for Publication Bias |journal=American Economic Review |volume=109 |issue=8 |pages=2766–2794 |doi=10.1257/aer.20180310}}</ref> A 2025 study using simulations and large-scale empirical applications reported that both can be biased by spurious precision (reported standard errors smaller than the data warrant) when it is related to the size of the estimated effect. It introduced the Meta-Analysis Instrumental Variable Estimator (MAIVE), which uses the inverse of the primary-study sample size as an instrument for the reported variance.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Irsova |first1=Zuzana |last2=Bom |first2=Pedro R. D. |last3=Havranek |first3=Tomas |last4=Rachinger |first4=Heiko |year=2025 |title=Spurious precision in meta-analysis of observational research |journal=Nature Communications |volume=16 |article-number=8454 |doi=10.1038/s41467-025-63261-0 |doi-access=free|pmc=12475282 }}</ref>

===Study registration===
{{Further|Registered report|Clinical trial registration}}
In September 2004, editors of prominent medical journals (including the ''[[New England Journal of Medicine]]'', ''[[The Lancet]]'', ''[[Annals of Internal Medicine]]'', and ''[[Journal of the American Medical Association|JAMA]]'') announced that they would no longer publish results of drug research sponsored by pharmaceutical companies unless that research was registered in a public [[clinical trials registry]] database from the start.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/politics/2004/09/09/journals-insist-drug-manufacturers-register-all-trials/37be9ce1-23fd-4b07-943c-73336c5375a1/ |title=Journals Insist Drug Manufacturers Register All Trials |last=Vedantam |first=Shankar |date=2004-09-09 |newspaper=Washington Post |access-date=2020-02-03 |language=en-US }}</ref> Furthermore, some journals (e.g. ''[[Trials (journal)|Trials]]),'' encourage publication of [[clinical trial protocol|study protocols]] in their journals.<ref name="Protocol">{{cite web |url=http://www.trialsjournal.com/info/instructions/?txt_jou_id=10096&txt_mst_id=61789 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20070802024936/http://trialsjournal.com/info/instructions/?txt_jou_id=10096&txt_mst_id=61789 |title=Instructions for Trials authors&nbsp;— Study protocol |date=2009-02-15|archive-date = 2007-08-02}}</ref>

The [[World Health Organization]] (WHO) agreed that basic information about all clinical trials should be registered at the study's inception and that this information should be publicly accessible through the WHO [[International Clinical Trials Registry Platform]]. Additionally, the public availability of complete study protocols, alongside reports of trials, is becoming more common for studies.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Dickersin| first1 = K.| last2 = Chalmers | first2 = I. | title = Recognizing, investigating and dealing with incomplete and biased reporting of clinical research: from Francis Bacon to the WHO | volume = 104 | issue = 12 | pages = 532–538 | date = 2011| pmid = 22179297 | doi=10.1258/jrsm.2011.11k042 | journal=J R Soc Med | pmc=3241511}}</ref>
